You could count her ribs and she liked that, she thought it was a trick, and she would pull her shirt up in front of guests to have it done and I would have to stop her.
Below the right shoulder blade there is a mole, small, slightly raised. On the top of the left shoulder there is nothing. I say that because people assume a list is only the things that are there.
The bitten nail on the right thumb and no other finger. The little finger that sat out away from the rest when she held a pencil, which the teacher tried to fix in the first year and gave up on.
The fold in the top of the left ear, which is his father’s ear.
The jaw that came forward when she was told something she did not accept.
The front teeth with the gap closing. It had about a year left in it.
The nose, which was going to be a nose.
The eyes — and I am not going to describe the eyes, because everybody describes the eyes, and it has become a thing people do at me in the street, and I will not join them.
The gap in the right eyebrow where she went into the door frame at five, no stitches, the hair never came back in a strip about as wide as a thread.
The hairline, high on the left, low on the right.

And the crown, where there are two whorls instead of one, which his grandmother said meant a long life, and which his mother said meant nothing, and which I have been told four separate things about by four separate women in this neighbourhood since Esfand.
That is the whole of it and I can do it in about four minutes if nobody interrupts me.
People assume it is a prayer. A woman put her hand on my arm at the market in Khordad and said, God accept it, because she had heard me doing it under my breath while I was choosing onions.
It is not a prayer. It is an inventory.

A body is a list, and after everything else has been taken off the table — the day, the hour, the building, the order it happened in, the number of them, the names on the number — the list is still mine. Nobody is reviewing it. Nobody is going to telephone me in a year and say the list has been revised.
Mansour cannot do it.
He has tried. I have heard him try, in the yard, at night, with the gate shut. He gets to the knees and he stops, and then he starts again at the feet, and he gets to the knees and he stops.
He says it is because he was always at work.
It is not because he was at work.
WHO DECIDED?
I was told that the matter was being looked at above the level of the province.
In Ordibehesht they put a table at the front of the Husseiniyeh and a man sat behind it.
His name was Āghā-ye Shafi’i and I want to say at the start that I have nothing against him, which is a sentence I have had to work at, and which took me about five months.
He came from the province. He had a folder. He had a younger man with him who did not speak and who wrote, and I have thought since that the younger man was the whole of it and the folder was for us.

He was not slippery. That is the thing nobody believes when I tell it. People want him to have been slippery, because a slippery man can be caught out, and there is a pleasure in catching a man out, and I was ready for that pleasure, I had been saving it up for two months.

He stood up when women came in. He drank the tea. He knew the name of the school and he said it correctly, with the right stress on it, which not one person from outside this province has managed since.
And he said: I am not going to tell you anything I have not been told.
Which is honest. It is so honest that it took me a week to work out that it is also the door closing.

I asked my question. I had written it down, which I had never done in my life, on the back of a receipt from the parts place in Bandar Abbas, because I knew that if I was standing up in a room with that many people in it I would lose the words.
I said: who decided.
And he looked at me and he did not look away, and he said that the matter was being looked at above the level of the province.
Then he gave me a card.

It is a small card, white, and it has a telephone number on it and a department, and he said: ring this and give them your name and the registration number of your case, and anything that comes down will come down through them.
I want to tell you about that number, because it is the thing from that whole year that I would take out of the world if I were allowed to take one thing out of it, and it is not the missile.
The number works.

I have rung it forty times. Not once has it rung out. Not once has a man been rude to me. There is a woman on it most mornings who knows my voice now, and asks after my son, and says āghā-ye and my family name in the way they teach you in a course, and she takes my name, and she reads my case number back to me, and she confirms it, and she says that there is nothing further on the file at this time.
Every single time. For eight months. With kindness. Correctly.

If a man had slammed a door in my face in Esfand I would have had a door. I have been given a woman who is sorry, in a department that exists, on a number that answers, and there is nothing on the other end of it, and there never was, and I rang it again on Tuesday.
They started the room in Farvardin, in the week when nobody had anywhere to be.

The first time there were about ninety of us standing because there were not enough chairs, and then somebody brought chairs from the school on the north side, which was a kind thing to do and which I have not been able to think about since.
For four weeks it was the only place I could breathe.

You have to understand what it is outside that room. Outside that room you are a woman people cross the street for. Not away from — toward. They come toward you with their faces already arranged, and they take your hand in both of their hands, and some of them cry, and you have to hold them up, and then you have to go home and cook.

Inside that room nobody arranges their face. You can say a flat, ugly thing — I did not like her very much in the autumn, she was a horror in the autumn — and a woman across the room nods, because her son was a horror in the autumn, and nobody tells you that God accepts anything.
So I went, and I spoke in the second week, and I slept afterwards, which I had not done.
I stopped in the fifth week.
This is the part I have not explained to my husband properly, and I have tried twice.
In the first week, Ozra said about her boy that he had been to the water on the Friday.
In the third week it was the Friday and he had sat at the front of the boat.
In the fifth week it was the Friday, and the front of the boat, and he had put his hand over the side, and he had looked back at her once from the front of the boat and not said anything.

She is not a liar. I want that down in the same ink as everything else. She is a woman who has lost a child and who sat for four weeks in a room with ninety people who were each handing round the best four minutes they had, and the four minutes go round, and they do not come back the same, and nobody in that room is doing anything except trying to keep hold of a child.
And I sat there in the fifth week and I heard my own Friday come out of another woman’s mouth, and I thought: in a year I will not know.
So I stopped going, and I have been called hard for it, and I am hard, and that was not why.
Mansour goes every week. He has not missed one. He says it helps.
It does help. That is the trouble with it.
WHY WAS THE SCHOOL OPEN?
I was told that a closure instruction had been issued at the discretion of the school and that its timing formed part of the review.
It took me until Khordad to find out that she did everything right.

Not from the card. Not from the table at the Husseiniyeh. From Mohsen, who drives for the clinic, whose wife’s cousin was in the office that morning and who is therefore, in this town, a primary source.
At about the hour, the head teacher understood what was happening before anybody in that building and before most people in this country, and she gave the instruction, and they began telephoning.

They telephoned in order. They had a book with the numbers in it and they went down the book, two of them, on the two telephones, and when a number did not answer they went on and came back to it, and the ones they got, they told to come.
My wife’s number is in that book. So is mine. The yard has a telephone on the wall by the compressor and it has been on the wall since the year I took the yard.
I did not hear it. The compressor was running.

My wife was in a shop with a tin in her hand and her telephone in the bag on her shoulder, and the bag was on the floor by the door, because that is where you put a bag in Reza’s shop, and the radio was loud, and it is eighteen minutes from Reza’s shop on foot.

Some of them got there. I want that in. Some parents got there and stood at the gate and were handed their children and took them home and they are at home now, and I have nothing in me at all about those parents, which is a thing I did not expect.
She got the instruction out, and she got the telephones going, and she got the little ones down the stairs and across, and she was still in the building.
So there it is.

The one person who did every single thing right, in the right order, faster than anybody would have done it, is dead, and cannot be thanked, and cannot be blamed, and has a mother of her own in this province who has had to listen to people in Tehran discuss whether the timing of her daughter’s instruction forms part of a review.
I had been carrying it since Esfand like a man carrying a crankcase across a yard, which you can do, you can carry a thing like that a long way if you know there is a bench at the other end.
There was no bench.
And it has to go somewhere. That is the thing nobody tells you. It is not a feeling, it is a weight, and a weight has to be put down on something, and for about two months I put it down on my wife.
He never said it.

I want to start there because if I do not start there it will sound like something it was not, and because in thirty years that man has not said a cruel thing to me, not once, not even in the bad year with the yard, not even when his father died.
He never said it. He handed me things.

He would come in at eight and wash and sit down and I would put the food in front of him and he would say thank you, and take the glass from my hand, and the thank you was correct and the glass was taken correctly, and every day for two months I was told, by a man being polite to me in my own kitchen, that I had been in a shop.

Buying oil for him. I have never said that to him. I have said it in my head perhaps four hundred times and I have never once said it out loud, and I am not going to, because the day I say it is the day it becomes true for both of us instead of only for me.

Zeynab knew. Twelve years old and she knew in the first week and she started doing a thing, which was to sit down at the table before her father did and talk at him, continuously, about nothing — a girl at her school, a problem with a bus — so that there was never a silence in that room for him to hand me a glass into.
She did it for two months. Nobody asked her to. We have never discussed it.
That is my eldest, who everybody in this family agrees is the difficult one.
And in Khordad I had enough, and I put the plate down harder than I meant to, and I said: say it.
He said: say what.
I said: say that if I had not been at Reza’s I would have had my telephone in my hand. Say it in this kitchen, out loud, once, and then we will both have heard it and we can get on.
And he sat there.

He is a man who can take a motor off a transom in the dark. He sat in that chair with his hands on the table and he could not get one sentence out of himself, and I watched him try and fail twice, and then he got up and went out to the yard.
And I stood at the sink and I heard the motor start.

There was nothing on the stand. I know what is on that stand, I have been married to that stand for thirty years, and it was empty, and he had put a motor in the tank and started it and was standing in the dark listening to it run for nothing at all.
IS GOD WATCHING US NOW?
She asked me that when she was six, in the dark, about something she had done to her sister. I said yes. I said it in the voice.
I am going to do this once and then I am not going to discuss it again.

I did not lose my faith. I want to be accurate, because people have been generous to me about this and their generosity has the word lost in it, and lost means I put the thing down somewhere and that it may yet turn up behind a cupboard.
What I had was a floor. I have written about the floor. You do not think about a floor. You think about a floor on the day you put your foot through one.
Here is what I did, in my own yard, in Khordad, with a motor running in the tank for no reason.
I said: all right.

I said: I am not going to ask you for her. I know that is not a thing that is done. In seven thousand years nobody has had one back and I am not a fool and I am not going to stand in a yard and ask for the one thing I know the answer to.
I said: I am asking you for a name.

That is all. I said it out loud, to the air above my own roof, with my hands on the tank. I said: tell me who decided. Not punish him. I have not asked you to punish him. I would like to know what to put my hand on. A name is a smaller thing than a miracle. A name costs you nothing. You have a whole book of them.
And then I said the other thing, which I have told nobody, and which my wife will read here for the first time.

I said: and if it was you, then say it was you, and I will take it from you, and I will never come to you again, and you will have lost one man out of a town of forty thousand and you will not notice, but I will know, and knowing is the thing I came for.
Nothing.
Not silence — silence would be an answer, silence is a thing a man does when he has heard you. Nothing. A motor running in a tank, and a dog two streets over, and the heat coming off the tin.
And I stood there with my hands wet and I understood what I had been doing for five months.

I have a card in my wallet with a telephone number on it, and I ring it, and a woman takes my name and reads my case number back to me correctly and says there is nothing further on the file at this time.

And I had just done it again. In my own yard. To the sky. Gave my name, gave the number of my case, asked for what was on the file, and was told, with great kindness, by a thing that exists and answers and has a department, that there is nothing further at this time.
I have been praying to a telephone number.
I went in at about one and my wife was awake and she did not ask me anything. I will put down what she did, because I think it is the best thing anybody has done for me in my life. She moved over.
HOW LONG WILL IT TAKE?
I was told that these things take time.
The journalist came in Khordad and I am going to set down how she worked, because it was the first thing in four months that I recognised.

She came twice before she asked me anything. The first time she drank tea in the yard for fifty minutes and asked me about the motors and let me talk, and I knew what she was doing and I did not mind, because I have done the same thing to a man about a gearcase when what I wanted was to see his hands.

She had a permit. She showed it to me without being asked, which nobody does. She had a man driving her up from Bandar Abbas and she paid him by the day and she told me what she paid him, and it was correct — it was neither the price a foreigner gets charged nor an insult.
She had two recorders. Not one. She put the small one on the bench between us and the other one stayed in her bag, running, and she told me that as well, at the start, the first time, before the tea.
She wrote in a book with a soft cover and she wrote with her left hand and she wrote while she was looking at me, which I have never seen anybody do.

She asked me the same thing four different ways over three visits and did not pretend she was not doing it. On the third visit she said: I am going to ask you about the telephone in the yard again, and I am going to ask it differently, and you are allowed to be annoyed with me.
She asked what time of day I service a gearcase and why. She asked how long the walk to the gate is and then she walked it with me and timed it, and then she walked it again.

She asked me what I did with my hands when Shafi’i gave me the card, and I said I did not know, and she said: you put it in your shirt pocket and then you moved it to your wallet before you left the building.

And she was paid by the word. She told me that too. I asked her and she told me, and then she told me the number of words, and the number was smaller than I expected and the money was larger than I expected, and we sat in that yard and did the arithmetic of it together on the back of a parts receipt like two men pricing a job.
I liked her. I want it on the record that I liked her and that I would have her in my yard again tomorrow, because of what I am going to have to say about her later.
She was the first person in four months who came into this house with a trade instead of a face.
On the fourth visit she asked me whether there was anything in the house in her handwriting.
The belongings came back in Tir, in a bag of the kind you take to a wedding.
I am not going to make a list of that one. One list is enough for any woman.
The exercise book was in it.

It should not have been in it. The exercise books stay in the desk, that is the whole point of them, and I have never had an explanation and I have never asked for one and I do not want one, because any explanation of how that book got into that bag is going to involve a sentence about where the desk was.

It is the thin kind with the soft cover. Squared paper, which they use for everything whether it suits the subject or not. Her name on the front in her own hand, which she did in the first week of every year with a ruler under the letters, and which is a thing she got from her sister and not from me.
And the composition is in it, the one about the tree, the one she was made to read out, and the mark is on it in red.
Eighteen out of twenty. And a line under the roots of a tree are the same size as the tree, you just cannot see them, and in the margin, in the teacher’s hand: good — but how do you know?
That is the only object in this world with the two of them on it.

Mansour has it in the drawer in the yard with the manuals, which I was angry about for a week and am not angry about any more, because that drawer is the driest place in this house and he knew that and I did not.
The journalist asked for it. Not to take — to photograph, on the bench, with the light from the door.
I said no.

I did not give her a reason and she did not ask for one and I have thought about that since, because a woman who asks the same question four ways did not ask that one twice, and I think she already knew she was going to be told no and had decided to be told no politely.
Mansour photographed it himself, with his telephone, badly, and sent it to her that night from the yard.

He has not mentioned it. He does not know that I know. He has sent that woman a photograph of the only thing in this house that is certainly my daughter’s and he has sat across a table from me for four months and not said so, and I have let him, and we are two people who have got very good at this.
WAS IT A MISTAKE?
I was told that the question of how the site came to be designated forms part of the review.
She told me in Mordad, in the yard, standing up, because she had a car waiting.

She said: I want to be straight with you. In a year I will not be able to tell you who decided, and I do not think anybody will ever be able to tell you that, and if a man tells you he can, write down his name and tell me.
I said I understood.
And she said: but I can tell you that somebody knew.

Years ago — seven, she said, before any of this, in an ordinary month, with no war on — a person whose job it was to look at buildings looked at that building and understood exactly what it had become. The paint. The gates. The two playgrounds. She said that person did not shrug. That person wrote it down, carefully, in the proper form of words, and put it where such a thing is put.
And the place it was put was not the place where the other thing was kept.
So the other thing — the old description of that building, from a time when it was true — sat where it had always sat, and nothing came along and corrected it, because nothing is anybody’s job.
I said: so there was a man.
She said: there was a person, and I will never have their name either.

Now I am going to put down what happened to me in my own yard with my hands in the water of the tank, because it is not what it should have been and I have had three months to make it sound better and I am not going to.
I was glad.

For about four seconds I was glad, because for five months what I had wanted, the thing I had asked the sky for, the thing I had been ringing a telephone number about, was a person who had looked at my daughter’s school and decided. And here he was. Here she was. Here was somebody who had looked at that building and seen it.
And then I understood that he had seen it, and had done the right thing, and had done it better than I would have done it, and had written it down, and had put it where it goes.
And it happened anyway.
I would like to explain what that is, in my own trade, because it is the only way I have of holding it.

I have rebuilt perhaps nine thousand motors. When a motor fails, there is a part. You can put the part on a bench and a man can stand over the bench and look at the part, and the part is the reason, and it can be shown to the owner, and the owner can be charged for it or not charged for it, and everybody in that yard knows where they are. Thirty years. Not once, not one single time in thirty years, has a motor failed and there been no part.
There is no part.

Every man in that chain did his own piece correctly. The one who looked wrote it down. The one who kept the description kept it as he had been given it. The one who pressed whatever was pressed had on his screen a thing that he had every right to believe. The machine that put it on his screen is not responsible for what was given to it, and that is not a lie, I have read it, it is a true sentence.
Every link held. The chain held. And there is nothing on the bench.

I have a man in this town — I will not say who, and I will not say the year — whose boy was taken by our own people and given back to him in a condition I am not going to describe. That man knows the name of the building. He knows the name of the man who signed the paper. He has a piece of paper with a signature on it. He has somewhere to stand.

I have been sitting with that for three months and I will probably sit with it for the rest of my life. He has less than me in every way a man can have less, and he has one thing I do not have, and I have caught myself envying him for it, and I would like to be a man who had not caught himself doing that.
On the third day they called us in.

Not all of us. In an order, by a list, and the list was the only one of all those lists that turned out to be real, and it was a list of what had been brought out and sorted, and we were called against it.

There was a table. There was a man at it from the forensic department who had not slept and who was being spoken to by four people at once and answering all four of them, and who was doing his job in a corridor with the doors open at both ends.
And there was a sheet of paper with two lines on it and a place for a name.
Above the place for my name was a sentence which said that I had identified her.

What was on that table was a shoe, and a piece of cloth from a coat that is made in quantity and sold in this province by the thousand, and one other thing, and I am not going to write down what the other thing was.
I knew the shoe.

I want that said first and said plainly: I knew the shoe, I knew it in the first half second, I had bought it, I had argued about the price of it, I had made her wear it when she wanted the other ones, and there was a crease across the top of the left one from the way she pushed her feet in without undoing them, and the crease was there.
I did not know the cloth. There are four hundred of those coats in this town.
I did not know the other thing. I had never seen it before in my life.
And on the second day, in the courtyard, I had watched a woman be told to wait.

Nothing cruel. A young man with a list and a kind face told her that there was nothing yet and that she should go home and that they would send for her, and she said she would wait, and she waited, and I saw her again that evening in the same place and she was still waiting and she was still being handled kindly, and something had begun to happen to her face that I have not seen on a face before or since.
Three of them were never found at all. We know that now. One boy’s mother has a sweater and one shoe and they are in a glass case in a mosque and she goes and stands in front of her son’s sweater.
So I looked at the man at the table, and I took the pen, and I put my name on the paper that said I had identified her.
I was certain of a shoe.

She was buried on the fourth day with her name on the stone and her father walking in front, and he has never once asked me what was on that table, and he will not, and if he ever reads this he will find out the way you are finding out.

In Tir the forensic department published what it had done, because they were proud of it and they were entitled to be proud of it — sixty-two pieces, identified by the laboratory, belonging to thirty-two children. They worked at it for seven months. They are good men and they did a thing almost nobody could have done.

So I know what is in that grave, which is: some of my daughter, and some of other people’s children, and the arithmetic of it does not work out any other way and I did it the night I read it, on the back of an envelope, at this table, and then I burned the envelope.

And I would do it again. That is the part I expect to be judged for and I accept the judgement in advance. I would sign it again tomorrow morning. I have a stone with her name on it and a day in the month when I go to it, and there is a woman two streets from here who has a glass case in a mosque, and I have looked at that woman across a room for eight months and I have never once wished we had changed places.
He goes on the Thursday.

He takes the folding chair out of the boot and he sits down and he talks to her for an hour about the business — about the Yamaha, about Hassan, about what the parts place in Bandar Abbas is charging now — exactly the way he went up to his father every Khordad and sat for an hour and told him about the business. He does not believe she can hear him. He has told me that himself, in this kitchen, with no feeling in it at all, the way he tells me the price of a coil.
And he goes every single week.
I let him.
WHICH ONES ARE MINE?
I did not ask this one on the telephone.

I am going to try to write down the thing that is wrong with me, and I have put it off for two months because I believe that writing it down will make it true, and I have been told that is not how it works, and I think the person who told me that has never written anything down.
In Tir they published the work the laboratory had done and it was in every house in this province inside a day, and I read it at the bench with the radio off.
I am not going to discuss the grave. My wife and I have between us one grave and one stone and a day in the month and I am not going to take a chisel to it in a book.
It is not the grave. I want to be understood. It is not the grave at all.
It is that I have been in a room since Farvardin.
Every week. Ninety of us at the start, sixty now, in a hall with chairs borrowed from another school, and we go round, and we each say the thing we have.

And what you have, after the first month, is the four minutes. Everybody arrives at their four minutes. Nobody chooses them — the four minutes choose you, and then they are what you have, and you bring them, and you hand them round, and you take everybody else’s.

I have been doing that for eight months. I have sat in that room, every week, and taken in another man’s Friday and another woman’s kitchen and a boy who held his breath for twelve and a girl who checked a dish of lentils twice a day and made a report of it, and some of them are mine and some of them were handed to me, and in the room it does not matter, in the room it is the kindest thing in this province.
And my daughter has been getting better.

That is the sentence. That is the whole of it. In Farvardin she was a nine-year-old with a crooked little finger who was a horror in the autumn, and in Aban she is — I have been trying to find the word — she is finished. She says the right thing at the end of a story. She has a line about the water being the same as the water at home. She has an answer about a dish of lentils that lands so well that a woman in that hall laughed out loud at it last month, and I took the laugh, and I have thought about the laugh every day since, because I do not know where that answer came from.
There is a day in the mud with the little fish.
There is an afternoon about the ice, and a thing she said about it afterwards that I have repeated perhaps two hundred times.
There is a girl at my elbow at a bowl of mahyawa asking me how many times I had made it and doing arithmetic at me about how many I had left.

I cannot certify one of them. Not one. I have sat in that yard with the gate shut and gone through them like a man going through a box of parts looking for the one that is stamped, and they are all the right shape and they all fit and not one of them is stamped, and the one I am least sure of is the one I love best, and I am not going to say which one it is, and that is the only decision I have made this year.
I have one thing.

It is a thin exercise book with squared paper, in the drawer in the yard with the manuals, because that drawer is the driest place on this property. Her name on the front with the letters done against a ruler. A composition about a tree. A mark in red in the corner — eighteen out of twenty — and a line under one sentence, and four words in the margin in another woman’s hand, and that other woman is dead too.
That is the whole of what I can prove about my daughter.
Here is what I do at night, and I have not told the room and I am not going to tell the room.

I know that building. I hung a door in it. I went up those stairs with a fan under my arm in the year the old one burned out and I stood in that room while a woman held the chair steady for me and complained about the noise, and I know where the windows are and I know that the boards run the long way and I know there are two desks against the back wall that are shorter than the others.
So I put them back.

I can do it. I know all their names now — that is what eight months in that hall gives you, you come out of it knowing ninety names and their birthdays and what they would not eat — and I sit in my own yard with the tin going cold over my head and I put them at the desks, one at a time, in the places they sat in, which I also know now, because the mothers have told each other.
And every desk has a child at it.

There is no empty one. I have been doing it since Mordad and I have never once found the empty desk, and I go along the rows to the end of the room and they are all there, all of them, every one, sitting up, and one of them is mine, and I cannot tell you which.
WHO DECIDED?
She came to the yard in Aban to say she was going.

Not finished. Going. She said the piece would run in the winter and that it would be about the description and the person who wrote the note and the place the note was put, and that it would not say who decided, because she still did not know and had stopped expecting to.
I said that was honest.

She said: there is something else, and I am going to tell you, and then I am going to tell you what I am going to do with it, and you are going to be angry with me, and I would rather you were angry with me in this yard than in a year’s time in a shop.
Then she told me what my wife signed on the third day.
I am not going to put down what I did. I was sitting on the drum by the tank and I stayed on the drum.

She had seen the paper. She had seen the whole list and she had seen a photograph of what was on that table, because she is good at her trade and she had spent five months being good at it in this province, and that is what you get.
And she said: I am not going to use it.

I said she had to. I said that if the thing that happened to us is ever going to be made to cost anybody anything, then that — the table, the three days, the shoe, a woman putting her name to a sentence she could not know was true — is the part that will do it, because it is the part a person in another country cannot argue with.
And she said: yes. And that is exactly why.

She said: if I write that, then in six weeks there is a number in it. There is a man on a screen somewhere using your wife to argue that the count is wrong, and another man using her to argue that it is right, and your wife becomes the reason a figure is disputed. Her name. Doing that work. For the rest of her life and after it.
She said: and the thing she did on the third day was the only thing anybody in this has done on purpose, and I am not going to turn it into evidence.

Then she said the thing that I have not been able to put down for three weeks, which is: I am sorry. I know what I am doing. I am the last person who is going to decide what may be said about your family, and I have decided, and you have no way of making me do otherwise, and I am aware of what that makes me.
And I sat on the drum in my own yard and I worked out that she was right.

I have spent eight months on a telephone asking men in offices to tell me something. There was exactly one person in the world who found something out and came and told me to my face. She is also the one person who has taken a thing about my family and locked it in a drawer and told me she is not giving it back.
Those are the same person. They are the same act. I have turned it over every way a man can turn a thing over and they do not come apart.

She shook my hand. She asked me to say goodbye to my wife, who would not come out of the kitchen, and who had known since Khordad exactly what that woman was and had said so, and whom I had told she was being unfair.
I went in at about seven.
My wife was at the sink with the radio on, and Younes was under the table with the dog, and Zeynab was doing the thing where she reads out loud to nobody.
I asked my wife if she wanted tea.
In thirty years that man has never once asked me if I wanted tea.

He makes tea. He is not a man who does not make tea. But the asking is mine, it has been mine since the first week of this marriage, it is the smallest and most fixed thing in this house, and he came in out of that yard at seven o’clock in Aban and stood in the door and asked me if I wanted tea.
So I knew.
I said yes.

And he made it, badly, the way he has made it for thirty years, and he brought it to the table and sat down, and we drank it, and Zeynab read out loud to nobody in the other room, and the boy fell asleep under the table and had to be carried, and he carried him.
And then he came back and sat down and he said: do the feet.
I said: what?
He said: the list. Do the feet.
And I did it.
I have done it under my breath in a shop while choosing onions and I have done it in the dark with my face in a cushion and I had never once done it out loud to another person.

I started at her feet, and I did the second toe that is longer than the first, which is mine, and the nails that grow crooked on the left, which are his, and the lentil of a scar on the outside of the left ankle, and I got to the knees.
And he did not stop me.

He sat there with his hands flat on the table and he let me come up past the knees, and past the mark on the thigh from the water heater, and the ribs you could count, and the bitten nail on the right thumb and no other finger, and the fold in the top of the left ear, which is his father’s ear, and the gap in the eyebrow the width of a thread, and all the way up to the crown, where there are two whorls instead of one.
And when I got to the two whorls he said: my grandmother said that meant a long life.
And I said: your mother said it meant nothing.

That is all. That is the whole of that evening. We sat in that kitchen for another hour and talked about a bill, and about whether Zeynab’s eyes need looking at again, and about a man who owes him for a coil since Esfand.

Neither of us said the other thing. There are two other things in this house now, one each, and we both know where both of them are, and we are not going to say them, not this year and not in ten years, and when one of us dies the other one will carry both.

People from outside think the unsaid thing is a silence. It is not a silence. It is work. It is the hardest work either of us has ever done and we do it every single day and we have got very good at it.
We can do it in about four minutes if nobody interrupts us.
The envelope comes home in the backpack on a Thursday, bent, with a juice stain on one corner.
Inside is a proof sheet. The whole class in four rows, the short ones kneeling at the front, a blue curtain behind them, and a boy on the end of the second row with his eyes shut.
There is an order form. Package A is the one print. Package
B is the one print and eight wallet size and a keyring and costs thirty-eight dollars. Package C has the magnet.
He puts the proof sheet on the counter under the car keys and reads the back of the form twice, because the deadline is
The girl wants to know if she can keep the proof sheet.
He says no, it goes back.
She asks again at dinner. He says it goes back, that’s how it works, they need it back.

He writes the check at the counter standing up, with his coat still on, and fills in the teacher’s name on the front of the envelope in block capitals, and puts it by the door with the library book so that it goes.
Outside, the sprinklers come on at the house across the street, and go off again, because it is October and nobody has reset them.
I found a gold one.
A gold what.
A bottle cap. The gold kind, from the orange drink, not the flat kind — the proper gold one with the inside still shiny.
Where.
By the ice place, in the dust at the side, and nobody had stepped on it. That is the whole thing. Usually they are stepped on.
What did you do.
I took it to my sister.
Why.
Because she is my sister.
But she is horrible to you. You said she was horrible to you.

She is. She waits until you are happy about a thing and then she says one sentence about it in an ordinary voice and the thing dies in your hand. She did it about my stone and she did it about the cup.
So why did you take her the bottle cap.
Because she is the one you take it to.
And what did she say.
She said: that is the best one. Where was it.
She did not.
She did. And then I told her where it was for a long time, and she listened to the whole of it, and she did not say anything at the end.
That is a good day.
It was a very good day. It was an ordinary Tuesday and it was one of the best days.
I have one like that.
Everybody has one like that. That is what I think. I think everybody has about four and nobody knows which four until after.
I worked out what the big girl said.
Go on then.
She said she was mine.
That is not it.
She said — all right — she said she was mine and that I had made her. And that she had been like that already, and I had made her more.
Made her more what?
That is the part I cannot do.
She said it kindly.
She said it very kindly. She was not telling me off.
Nobody has been told off yet, then.
Not yet.
I have thought of something and I do not know who to give it to.
Give it here.
When they find out — when somebody goes and tells the big one, and it is sorted out, and the person who made the mistake is told off properly —
Yes.
Will somebody come and tell us?

GLOSSARY
Aban [aa-BAAN] — The eighth month of the Solar Hijri year, late
October to late November.
Āghā [aa-GHAA] — Persian, sir, mister. The ordinary honorific, placed before a family name in the possessive form Āghā-ye.
Ajil [aa-JEEL] — Persian, nuts and dried fruit. The mixed bowl — pistachios, almonds, raisins, chickpeas, melon and pumpkin seeds — set out for guests and eaten through the long night of
Shab-e Yalda.
Alhamdulillah [al-ham-doo-li-LAAH] — Arabic, praise be to God.
Said on a thing going right, down to a motor turning over at the first pull.
Anshā [en-SHAA] — Persian, composition. The school essay exercise, set on an assigned subject and marked out of twenty.
Azar [aa-ZAR] — The ninth month of the Solar Hijri year, late
November to late December.
Bahman [bah-MAN] — The month between Dey and Esfand in the
Solar Hijri year, late January to late February.

Bandar Abbas [ban-DAR ab-BAAS] — The port city and provincial capital of Hormozgan, about a hundred kilometres west along the coast; the nearest city of any size, and the furthest this book’s father has ever been.
Boregheh [bo-re-GHEH] — Persian (Bandari), mask. The stiff embroidered face mask worn by older women on the southern coast, worked in indigo and gold thread, covering the brow, nose and upper lip.
Dey [DAY] — The tenth month of the Solar Hijri year, late
December to late January.
Esfand [es-FAND] — The twelfth and last month of the Solar Hijri year, late February to late March, ending at the spring equinox.
Farvardin [far-var-DEEN] — The first month of the Solar Hijri year, late March to late April.
Gearcase — The sealed lower housing of an outboard motor, holding the gears and the propeller shaft; the heaviest single thing a man in that trade lifts by himself.

Hafez [haa-FEZ] — The fourteenth-century poet of Shiraz. His collected poems are kept in most houses and opened at random on the long night of Shab-e Yalda, the poem landed on being read as an answer.
Hormozgan [hor-moz-GAAN] — The southern coastal province of
Iran, on the Strait of Hormuz, hot and humid, with a trading and seafaring culture of its own and a Persian spoken differently from the Persian of the capital.
Husseiniyeh [ho-sey-nee-YEH] — Arabic via Persian, the place of

Hussein. A hall, plainer than a mosque and used for assembly rather than prayer: mourning gatherings, recitations, the business of a neighbourhood, and the place a town puts a table when it has something to tell a great many people at once.
Impeller — The soft rubber-vaned rotor of an outboard’s water pump. It wears, it is replaced on a schedule, and when it fails the motor overheats within minutes.
Inshallah [een-shaa-LAAH] — Arabic, if God wills. Attached to any statement about the future, and meaning anything from a promise to a refusal depending entirely on how it is said.
Jiroft [jee-ROFT] — An inland town in Kerman province, about two hundred kilometres north, far enough from the coast and from anything worth striking to count as somewhere to send a family.
Kerman [ker-MAAN] — The province and city inland to the north; here, the road that runs that way out of town.
Khordad [khor-DAAD] — The third month of the Solar Hijri year, late May to late June.

Mahyawa [maah-YAA-wa] — Persian (Bandari), fish water. A thin dark sauce of fermented anchovy, salt, mustard seed and fennel, made along this coast and nowhere else in the country; eaten with bread, and the single thing a southerner abroad asks for.
Mehr [MEHR] — The seventh month of the Solar Hijri year, late
September to late October; the month the school year begins.
Minab [mee-NAAB] — A town of some fifty thousand in Hormozgan province, inland of the coast road east of Bandar Abbas, known for its Thursday market, its palm groves and its date harvest.
Mordad [mor-DAAD] — The fifth month of the Solar Hijri year, late
July to late August.
Nissan [nee-SAAN] — In Iran, any small flatbed pickup, after the
Nissan Junior assembled in the country for decades. The standard vehicle for moving anything heavy and awkward, an outboard motor included.
Nowruz [now-ROOZ] — Persian, new day. The new year, falling at the spring equinox at the end of Esfand, prepared for across three weeks of taking the house apart and cleaning it from the top down.
Ordibehesht [or-dee-be-HESHT] — The second month of the Solar
Hijri year, late April to late May.
Pashmak [pash-MAK] — Persian, candy floss. Here, a dog.

Ramazan [ra-ma-ZAAN] — Arabic via Persian, the ninth month of the lunar Islamic calendar, kept as a month of fasting from first light to sunset. Not a month of the Solar Hijri year, and so falling at a different season each year.
Sabzeh [sab-ZEH] — Persian, greenery. Wheat, lentils or barley sprouted in a dish in the weeks before Nowruz and set on the new year’s table; grown at home, because buying one is cheating.
Shab-e Yalda [shab-e yal-DAA] — Persian, the night of Yalda, from the Syriac for birth. The longest night of the year, at the end of
Azar, kept awake through with family, red fruit, ajil and Hafez, on the understanding that from here the light comes back.
Shahrivar [shah-ree-VAR] — The sixth month of the Solar Hijri year, late August to late September.
Shajareh Tayyebeh [sha-ja-REH tay-yee-BEH] — Arabic via
Persian, the goodly tree. A common name for a school, from the
Qur’anic likeness of a good word to a good tree, its root firm and its branches in the sky.

Telltale — The small hole in an outboard’s housing that spits a stream of cooling water when the pump is working. No stream means stop at once. It is the only part of the machine that tells you anything.
Tir [TEER] — The fourth month of the Solar Hijri year, late June to late July.
Transom — The flat board across a boat’s stern that an outboard motor clamps to.
Two-stroke — The engine cycle used by most small outboards, in which the lubricating oil is mixed into the fuel rather than held in a sump; hence the separate tin of oil, bought by the half-litre.
